content_voiceover: This dense diagram covers cellular iron metabolism and drug targets. In the duodenal enterocyte, DMT1 imports ferrous iron into the labile iron pool, which branches to ferritin storage or export via ferroportin, coupled with ceruloplasmin oxidizing iron for transferrin binding. On the left, reticuloendothelial cells recycle iron from erythrophagocytosis, and also import it via transferrin receptor 1 through the endosomal pathway using STEAP and DMT1. This is where the iron sensor complex lives, TfR2, HFE, hemojuvelin, and BMPR, which regulate hepcidin, and this exact complex is disrupted in hereditary hemochromatosis. On the right, the erythrocyte imports iron through mitochondrial Mfrn for heme synthesis, using frataxin, GRX5, ISCU, and ISD11 to build iron-sulfur clusters, and ferrochelatase inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to make heme. Heme is recycled through hemoglobin-haptoglobin via CD163 and heme-hemopexin via CD91. The exam takeaway: mutations in HFE, hemojuvelin, TfR2, or hepcidin cause hereditary hemochromatosis, while defects in the iron-sulfur cluster machinery cause sideroblastic anemias.
keypoints: Iron sensor complex (HFE, HJV, TfR2, BMPR) regulates hepcidin — mutated in hereditary hemochromatosis
Enterocyte/macrophage: DMT1 uptake → labile iron pool → ferritin (storage) or ferroportin (export)
Erythrocyte mitochondrion: Mfrn imports iron; FXN/GRX5/ISCU/ISD11 build Fe-S clusters; FECH makes heme
Fe-S cluster machinery defects → sideroblastic anemia
keypoint_voiceover: For boards, focus on two clinical links. The iron sensor complex, HFE, hemojuvelin, TfR2, and BMPR, controls hepcidin, and mutations here cause hereditary hemochromatosis. In the erythrocyte mitochondrion, frataxin, ISCU, and ISD11 build iron-sulfur clusters and ferrochelatase makes heme, and defects in this machinery cause sideroblastic anemias. Also remember ferroportin is the universal iron export channel, and it's the target hepcidin blocks.
